definition: One of the five eternal entities the Vachanamrut names (jīva, īśvara, māyā, brahma, parabrahma). Īśvaras are souls of a higher order who preside over cosmic bodies and functions, such as Virāṭ, Sūtrātmā and Avyākṛta. Like jīvas they are bound by māyā until God frees them. In ordinary usage the word, and especially parameśvar, simply means God.

The individual self: eternal, conscious and extremely subtle. It dwells in the heart and pervades the body through its consciousness. Ignorance (māyā) binds it to the body and to rebirth. It is freed by knowing itself as distinct from the body and by taking refuge in God.

gloss: God's power of delusion and the stuff of the world
definition: The power of God from which the material world of three guṇas is produced, and which makes souls identify with the body. The very first discourse also gives a devotee's definition: whatever comes between the mind and the form of God during meditation is māyā.

Brahman, the luminous, imperishable reality beyond māyā. The Vachanamrut often uses it for Akṣarabrahma and urges the devotee to become 'brahmarūp', identified with Brahman, while still offering devotion to God. It is distinct from Brahmā, the four-faced creator deity (બ્રહ્મા).
The supreme Brahman beyond Brahman/Akṣara: Puruṣottama Nārāyaṇa himself, the all-doer and the cause of every cause.

Literally 'that which does not perish'. The Vachanamrut describes Akṣara as having two forms: a formless, all-pervading expanse of consciousness (cidākāśa), which is God's abode, and a personal form that remains in God's service. Akṣaradhāma is the divine abode where God resides with the liberated.

God as the highest person, beyond both the perishable and the imperishable (the term comes from Gītā 15). The text stresses that he always has a divine form, is the controller and inner witness of all, and is the source of the avatāras.
The most frequent name for God in the text. Very often it refers to the manifest form of God present before the assembly, whom the devotee is urged to recognise and serve.
The conscious self, distinct from the three bodies, the three states (waking, dream, deep sleep) and the three guṇas. Seeing oneself as the ātmā rather than the body is called ātmaniṣṭhā.
Firm identification with one's own self as distinct from body and mind. With dharma, vairāgya and bhakti it is one of the four qualities of the single-minded (ekāntik) devotee.

Loving worship of God joined with knowledge of his greatness. The text names the nine forms of devotion (hearing, singing, remembering, serving and the rest). Devotion without understanding of God's greatness is described as weak.
Duty and moral conduct as taught in scripture. For the devotee it especially means svadharma, the vows proper to one's station: non-violence, celibacy for renunciants, truthfulness and the like.
Knowledge of the self as distinct from the body and knowledge of God's true form and greatness. The text warns against knowledge that is used as a pretext to drop dharma.
Non-attachment to sense-objects and worldly pleasure. The second discourse of the first Gadhada section grades it into superior, middling and inferior detachment.
Wholly devoted to God alone. The ekāntik devotee combines dharma, jñāna, vairāgya and bhakti with knowledge of God's greatness. Such conduct is called ekāntik dharma.
Understanding of the greatness of God and of his devotees. The text repeatedly says that devotion should always be accompanied by this understanding.
Firm conviction that the manifest form of God is God himself. It is described as the root of liberation and is said to grow or weaken with company and understanding.
Worship grounded in a correct understanding of God's form. Strong upāsanā means holding that God always has a divine form, even in his abode.

Association with what is true. A footnote in this edition explains sat as four things: God, the holy person (satpuruṣa), true dharma and true scripture. The word also names the fellowship of devotees.
A saintly devotee in whom God's virtues are seen. Serving such a person and avoiding faults toward them is described as an open door to God.
The soul's final good: release from māyā and attaining God's abode. Mokṣa and mukti are used in the same sense.
A soul freed from māyā who lives in God's abode in a divine body and serves God.
Deep-rooted desire for sense-objects, the seed of rebirth. The text treats overcoming it through vairāgya and devotion as a central struggle.
The four inner faculties: mind (man), intellect (buddhi), contemplation (citta) and ego (ahaṁkāra). Their states are analysed in many discourses.
The ten senses, five of perception and five of action, through which the soul engages with sense-objects (viṣaya).
The objects of the senses: sound, touch, sight, taste and smell (the 'five viṣayas'). Attachment to them is the main obstacle the text addresses.
Either a virtue, or one of the three qualities of māyā (sattva, rajas, tamas) that shape mind and states of consciousness.
Time as a power of God that brings change and dissolution. Together with karma and māyā it is said to have no power over the one who takes refuge in God.
Action and the merit or demerit it produces, which binds the soul to bodies and births.
Primordial matter. Paired with puruṣa in the account of creation (Mūla-puruṣa and Mūla-prakṛti), from whom the cosmic principles evolve.
A form God takes on earth for a purpose. The text holds the supreme God to be the source of all avatāras.
The form of God, whether manifest, in the abode, or in an image, and the focus of meditation and devotion.
Steady contemplation of God's form. Several discourses describe its practice and the obstacles to it.
The transcendent dwelling of God where liberated souls serve him. It is variously named Akṣaradhāma, Golok, Vaikuṇṭha or Brahmamahol.
Trance or absorption in which outward awareness ceases. The text values right understanding and conduct above samādhi alone.
Anvaya means God pervading and sustaining everything. Vyatireka means God remaining distinct from and beyond everything. The pair recurs in discussions of jīva, īśvara, māyā and Brahman.
Having a form, as opposed to nirākār, formless. The text insists that God is ever sākār and that his formless light is his effulgence.
The cosmic form or presiding īśvara of the gross universe, discussed alongside Sūtrātmā (subtle) and Avyākṛta (causal).
